svg.title: Bethell Laid to Rest at Yanghwajin
svg.desc:
GYEONGSEONG, May 1909 — Bethell Laid to Rest at Yanghwajin
Ernest Bethell, the British journalist who founded the Korea Daily News and sharply criticized Japanese encroachment, died on the 1st at the age of 37. He succumbed to heart disease at his Gyeongseong home. Large numbers of Koreans attended the funeral, and he was buried at Yanghwajin's foreign cemetery.
Bethell came to Korea to cover the Russo-Japanese War. In 1904 he established the newspaper with Yang Gi-tak and others. Its British publisher allowed it to evade Japanese censorship, exposing the injustice of the 1905 protectorate treaty. Its vigorous support for the National Debt Repayment Movement won a wide Korean readership. Japan twice pursued him through British consular courts. He received a custodial sentence and also served time in Shanghai.
Before his death he reportedly urged that, although he might die, the newspaper should live on to help the Korean people. Newspaper staff, students and merchants followed the funeral procession in tears.
Yanghwajin became a burial place for foreigners who died in Korea after the American physician Heron was interred there in 1890. At the death of a British man now resting on a hill overlooking the Han River, Koreans mourn the loss of another person who fought for their country. AI historical reconstruction; not an archival photograph.

SEOUL TIMES
Bethell Laid to
Rest at Yanghwajin
AI historical reconstruction; not an archival photograph.
Ernest Bethell, the British journalist who founded the
Korea Daily News and sharply criticized Japanese
encroachment, died on the 1st at the age of 37. He
succumbed to heart disease at his Gyeongseong home.
Large numbers of Koreans attended the funeral, and he
was buried at Yanghwajin's foreign cemetery.
Bethell came to Korea to cover the Russo-Japanese War.
In 1904 he established the newspaper with Yang Gi-tak
and others. Its British publisher allowed it to evade
Japanese censorship, exposing the injustice of the 1905
protectorate treaty. Its vigorous support for the
National Debt Repayment Movement won a wide Korean
readership. Japan twice pursued him through British
consular courts. He received a custodial sentence and

might die, the newspaper should live on to help the

Yanghwajin became a burial place for foreigners who
died in Korea after the American physician Heron was
